default.q.700_moji_n3-t9-q5.explanation: The noun 「品物」(しなもの) combines two kanji that are both read with kun-readings (品 - しな and 物 - もの). It refers to a concrete object that can be held, exchanged, bought, sold, or given as a present. Unlike 「商品」(しょうひん), which refers broadly to commercial merchandise, 「品物」focuses on the tangible object itself in everyday life. The sentence combines 「なかなか～ない」(very difficult to do something) with 「手に入る」(to obtain), meaning: “This is an item that is very difficult to find and buy nowadays.” Similar example: 「お礼として心のこもった品物を贈りました。」 (“I gave a heartfelt gift as a token of my thanks.”) Although both kanji often appear with on-readings in compounds such as 作品 and 動物, when combined as 品物, they are both read with their native Japanese readings: 「しな・もの」.

Its short negative form is 「慌てない」. The complete sentence means: "He is a very calm person and never panics, no matter what the circumstances are." For comparison: 「面接で難しい質問をされても、慌てずに笑顔で答えましょう。」 (Even if you are asked a difficult question in an interview, answer with a smile without panicking.) In the JLPT, distinguish 「慌てる」, becoming flustered after losing composure in an incident, from the easily confused 「焦る」（あせる）, becoming impatient or anxious under time pressure. default.q.700_moji_n3-t9-q7.explanation: 「険しい」 is a typical い-adjective in the N3 curriculum. It directly modifies nouns to describe steep, rough, and dangerous mountain terrain or roads, and can also be used figuratively for a tense expression or a difficult future. In 「（険しい）山道が続いている。」, it combines with 「山道」 to mean: "The rugged mountain road continues on." Another example is: 「初心者にとってこの険しいコースは危険すぎる。」 (For beginners, this rugged course is far too dangerous.) It is entirely different from 「怪しい」 (suspicious), 「苦しい」 (painful/difficult), and 「親しい」 (close/familiar).
